questions.prompt: What happened when Surveyor 3 came down toward the Moon?

choices.text: It touched down three times, bouncing twice before it stayed put
It landed gently on the first try and never moved
It bounced ten times across the Moon
It missed the Moon and kept flying

questions.explanation: Shiny rocks confused the descent radar, so the engine did not shut off at the right moment. Surveyor 3 bounced twice and settled on its third touchdown.

questions.prompt: What did Surveyor 3's digging show about the lunar soil?

choices.text: It was as hard as solid steel
It was a deep pool of liquid
It felt like wet sand and was strong enough to support an Apollo lunar module
It was too soft for anything to stand on

questions.explanation: Surveyor 3 dug four trenches and ran bearing and impact tests. Scientists decided the soil had a consistency like wet sand and was solid enough for an Apollo lunar module.

questions.prompt: Why did Surveyor 3 go silent after the lunar night began?

choices.text: It ran on sunlight, and the sunlight was gone
It ran out of television pictures to send
Its scoop arm broke off
It fell into a deeper crater

questions.explanation: Surveyor 3 was solar powered. After it sent 6,326 pictures, the lunar night left it in the dark, and NASA made its last contact on May 4, 1967.

questions.prompt: What did Neil Armstrong do when he saw Eagle was headed for a field of boulders?

choices.text: He took manual control and flew past a crater and the rocks
He turned around and flew back to orbit
He let the computer land on the boulders
He waited for Houston to take over the flying

questions.explanation: The guidance computer flashed 1202 and 1201 alarms because it was overloaded. Mission Control judged it safe to continue, and Armstrong flew manually over the boulder field before landing.

questions.prompt: What happened to Eagle's descent stage when the astronauts left the Moon?

choices.text: It flew back to Earth with them
It stayed behind on the Moon
It was thrown into the Sun
It orbited the Moon for years

questions.explanation: The crew climbed back into the ascent stage and lifted off. The descent stage stayed at Tranquility Base, after a lunar surface stay of about 21.6 hours.

questions.prompt: What do laser measurements bounced off the Apollo 11 reflector show about the Moon?

choices.text: The Moon is moving closer to Earth
The Moon is not moving at all
The Moon is shrinking by 3.8 centimeters a year
The Moon is moving farther from Earth by about 3.8 centimeters each year

questions.explanation: The reflector has 100 quartz glass prisms and needs no power. Scientists time how long laser light takes to return, and the distance grows by about 3.8 centimeters (1.5 inches) a year.

questions.prompt: Why did scientists choose Taurus-Littrow Valley for the Apollo 17 landing?

choices.text: It was the flattest place on the Moon
Rocks both older and younger than earlier samples might be found there
It was the closest spot to Earth
Water ice was already known to be there

questions.explanation: Taurus-Littrow was picked as a place where rocks older and younger than earlier Apollo and Luna samples might be found. Challenger landed there on December 11, 1972.

questions.prompt: What is the orange soil that Harrison Schmitt spotted near Shorty Crater made of?

choices.text: Rusty iron dust blown in from Mars
Crushed orange crystals from a meteorite
Paint from the lunar module
Tiny glass beads formed from sprays of lava about 3.5 billion years ago

questions.explanation: The orange soil is made of tiny glass beads that formed from lava sprays. It is better described as a volcanic ash than a soil.

questions.prompt: About how much lunar material did the Apollo 17 astronauts gather?

choices.text: About 110 kilograms (243 pounds)
About 1 kilogram
About 10 kilograms
About 1,000 kilograms

questions.explanation: The crew gathered 110.4 kilograms (243 pounds) of material, a record Apollo haul that scientists still study today.

questions.prompt: What made Viking 1 the first truly successful NASA landing on Mars?

choices.text: It was the first lander to reach Mars, and it landed exactly on target
An earlier lander, Mars 3, touched down in 1971 but lost contact within seconds, while Viking 1 kept working
It landed in 1971, before any other lander
It landed on the Moon first and then flew on to Mars

questions.explanation: The Soviet Mars 3 lander touched down in 1971, but contact was lost seconds later. Viking 1 landed on July 20, 1976, about 28 kilometers (17 miles) from its planned target.

questions.prompt: What did Viking 1's first color image show about Mars?

choices.text: Blue oceans under a clear sky
Green fields and tall trees
Orange-red ground under a sky with a reddish cast
White snow covering the whole plain

questions.explanation: The image was taken on July 21, 1976. The sky looks reddish, probably because reddish sediment hangs in the lower atmosphere.

questions.prompt: What did Viking 1's main test for organic compounds find in the Martian soil?

choices.text: Plenty of organic compounds, which proved life exists
A negative result, even though the combined data from four samples could be read as a weak sign of life
Only frozen water
Nothing, because the robot arm could not reach the soil

questions.explanation: On July 28, 1976, the robot arm dropped soil samples into the biological laboratory. The combined data from four samples could have been read as a weak positive for life, but the organic compounds test was negative.

questions.prompt: What did Opportunity find inside the BB-sized spheres nicknamed blueberries?

choices.text: Liquid water
Hematite, an iron mineral that often forms in water
Tiny fossils of Martian plants
Pure gold

questions.explanation: One of Opportunity's instruments showed the spheres contain hematite. Together with Spirit's findings, this helped confirm that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.

questions.prompt: Opportunity was built for a 90-sol mission. About how much longer than planned did it last?

choices.text: About twice as long
About 10 times as long
About 60 times as long
It stopped working right on schedule

questions.explanation: Opportunity kept rolling for more than 14 years, about 60 times longer than planned, and drove 45.16 kilometers (28.06 miles).

choices.text: A Mars-wide dust storm blocked its sunlight, and it never answered after its last signal
It drove off the rim of Endeavour Crater
Its airbags failed on landing
NASA turned it off after 90 sols

questions.explanation: Opportunity's last signal came on June 10, 2018. After more than a thousand commands got no answer, NASA declared the mission complete on February 13, 2019.

questions.prompt: What was special about the first likely marsquake that InSight recorded on April 6, 2019?

choices.text: It was caused by the lander's own landing
It was the first trembling that appeared to come from inside the planet
It destroyed the seismometer
It came from a space rock hitting the surface

questions.explanation: InSight landed on November 26, 2018. Its seismometer recorded the first likely marsquake on the lander's 128th Martian day, and it seemed to come from inside Mars.

questions.prompt: Why could InSight's mole not dig down about 5 meters as planned?

choices.text: The soil was clumpy and gave it too little friction
The ground was solid ice
The mole ran out of power
Its tether was cut by a marsquake

questions.explanation: The mole was designed for loose, sandy soil. It ended up just under the surface, but it still gathered data on the soil's physical and thermal properties.

questions.prompt: How did dust change InSight's solar panels between landing and 2022?

choices.text: Their energy rose from about 500 to about 5,000 watt-hours per sol
Their energy stayed about the same
Their energy fell from about 5,000 to about 500 watt-hours per sol
Their energy fell from about 50,000 to about 5,000 watt-hours per sol

questions.explanation: Dust slowly covered the panels. The last contact with Earth came on December 15, 2022, and NASA retired the mission on December 21, 2022.
